Learning outcomes
  • Apply the order of mathematical operations correctly.
  • Use R as a calculator.
  • Write R code to evaluate mathematical expressions.
``` ## Order of mathematical operations {#sec-1} - Mathematical operations are evaluated from left to right in a specific order. - Parentheses are evaluated first, then exponents, then multiplication and division, and finally addition and subtraction (@fig-order-operations). ![Order of mathematical operations](/images/operations-flow.jpg){#fig-order-operations fig-align="center" width="900"} - This sequence is often remembered using the acronym **PEMDAS**. ::: callout-note ## Operations with the same precedence - When operations have the same precedence (e.g., multiplication and division, or addition and subtraction), they are evaluated according to the order they appear from left to right. ::: ::::: panel-tabset ## Example M.1.1 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Calculate: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{2\times(3+4)-6 \times 4^2}$ $$2 \times(3+4)-6 \times 4^2 =$$ $$2 \times(7)-6 \times 4^2=$$ $$2 \times(7)-6 \times 16 =$$ $$14-96= -82$$ ## [Exercise M.1.1 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} ::: {#tabset-M11} Calculate: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\left( 3+\frac{4}{2} \right)^3-\sqrt{4\times9}\times2+2}$ :::
$$(3+\frac{4}{2})^3-\sqrt{4\times9}\times2+2 =$$ $$(3+2)^3-\sqrt{4\times9}\times2+2 =$$ $$(5)^3-\sqrt{4\times9}\times2+2=$$ $$125-\sqrt{4\times9}\times2+2=$$ $$125-\sqrt{36}\times2+2=$$ $$125-6\times2+2=$$ $$125-12+2=115$$
## [Exercise M.1.2 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} ::: {#tabset-M12} Calculate: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\frac{1^2+5^2+7}{4-1}}$ ::: The answer is ::::: ## Using R as calculator {#calculator} - R can be used as a calculator to evaluate different mathematical expressions. - The most common arithmetic operators in R are shown in @tbl-r-operators :::::: grid ::: g-col-2 ::: ::: g-col-8 | Operation | Operator | |----|:--:| | Addition | $+$ | | Subtraction | $-$ | | Multiplication | $*$ | | Division | $/$ | | Exponentiation | \^ or $**$ | | Integer division (returns result as integer discarding any remainder) | $\text{\%/\%}$ | | Modulo (returns the remainder of division) | $\text{\%\%}$ | : Table of arithmetic operators in R ::: ::: g-col-2 ::: ::::::
- Now, let's try to calculate the expression in @tabset-M11 using R and check that it gives the same answer: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Option 1: raising to the power 0.5 (3+4/2)^3-(4*9)^0.5*2+2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 115 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Option 2: using sqrt() function (3+4/2)^3-sqrt(4*9)*2+2 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 115 ``` ::: :::
::: panel-tabset ## Example M.1.2 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} - In this example, we will see how to perform ordinary division, integer division, and modulo operations in R. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # Ordinary division 10 / 3 # returns the result of the division (3.333333) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3.333333 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Integer division 10 %/% 3 # returns the integer quotient (3) discarding the remainder ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 3 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Modulo 10 %% 3 # returns the remainder of the division (1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 1 ``` ::: ::: ## Example M.1.3 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} - In this example, we will see how operations with the same precedence are evaluated. ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} 4/2*3 ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 6 ``` ::: ::: - In this expression, both division and multiplication have the same precedence. However, division is performed before multiplication **because it appears first from left to right**. ## [Exercise M.1.3 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} Write R code to calculate @tabset-M12. ::: {.cell webex.hide='Click to show/hide answer'}
```{.r .cell-code} (1^2+5^2+7)/(4-1) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 11 ``` :::
::: ::: ## Key points - Parentheses make the intended order of calculation explicit. - Multiplication and division have the same precedence and are evaluated from left to right. - Addition and subtraction also have the same precedence and are evaluated from left to right. - In R, use `%/%` for integer division and `%%` for the remainder. ## References - Bougioukas, K., I.
